Load inputs/gl2003-replication-processed-2023-03-28.csv
Load inputs/gl2003-replication-processed-2024-05-23.csv
Load inputs/readme.txt

Compute the original negative-expectation effect size by deriving f, eta-squared and the 90% CI from the reported F(1,156)=12.09, MSE=3.30, p=.001, r^2=.07 and N=160 using esc::esc_f and MBESS::ci.pvaf.
steps.quote: "[t]he affective reactions of the negative-expectation participants were less positive than those of the no-expectation participants, regardless of their level of need for cognition, F(1, 156) = 12.09, MSE = 3.30, p = .001, r² = .07", f = 0.270, η² = .07, 90% CI [.02, .14] (p. 317)

steps.summary: Compute the original expectation x NFC interaction effect size by deriving f, eta-squared and the 90% CI from the reported F(1,154)=6.40, MSE=3.21, p=.01, r^2=.04 and N=160 using esc::esc_f and MBESS::ci.pvaf.
steps.quote: "relative to no-expectation participants, the affective reactions of those in the positive-expectation condition became more positive as the need for cognition decreased (i.e., an assimilation effect), and less positive as level of need for cognition increased (i.e., a contrast effect), F(1, 154) = 6.40, MSE = 3.21, p = .01, r² = .04", f = 0.200, η² = .04, 90% CI [.005, .10] (p. 318, N = 160)

steps.summary: Compute the total sample size needed to achieve 95% power for the smaller effect of f=0.2 using pwr.anova.test with 3 groups (390 participants).
steps.quote: To achieve 95% power for the smaller of these two effects of f = 0.2, we would have needed 390 participants.

steps.summary: Round the required sample size up to N=400 and compute the multiple of the original sample size (400/160 = 2.5).
steps.quote: We rounded this number to N = 400 (see https://osf.io/6ua4s for the preregistered power analysis code), which corresponds to 2.5 times the original sample size.

steps.summary: Load the raw data, keep only interview-mode rows, recode -9 to missing, compute the affect index as the mean of the three affect items (BK01_01..03), compute the NFC score as the mean of the 16 German NFC items, recode the experimental condition (RD01) into positive/negative/none, and apply the exclusion criteria retaining only participants with non-missing NFC, affect index and experimental condition.
steps.quote: At first, the preregistered exclusion criteria were applied. Participants were excluded if values for any of the following variables were not available: Need for cognition, affect index, experimental group (assigned automatically during the experiment).

steps.summary: Compute the achieved statistical power for f=0.2 with the achieved sample size, the detectable effect size at 95% power, and the achieved power for the original f=0.200, using pwr.anova.test with 3 groups.
steps.quote: Achieved power was thus 81.37% for f = 0.2. This sample size is sufficient to detect effects of f = 0.249 with 95% power. The achieved power for the original effect size of f = 0.200 was 81.37%.

steps.summary: Compute age descriptives: count participants who reported age, count missing values, and compute mean, SD, min and max age.
steps.quote: Only 138 participants reported their age (114 missing values). The reported mean age was M = 47.11 (SD = 16.48) with a range from 19 to 77.

steps.summary: Tabulate gender: count male, female, diverse participants, those who did not want to disclose, and missing values.
steps.quote: 76 male, 169 female and four diverse persons participated in the study (2 did not want to disclose, 1 missing value).

steps.summary: Tabulate occupation: count students, apprentices, employed, in search of employment, retired, and missing values.
steps.quote: 31 participants reported that they were either bachelor- or master students, while only one person was in an apprenticeship. 153 subjects were employed, 5 in search for employment, and 61 in retirement (1 missing value).

steps.summary: Compute Cronbach's alpha for the 3-item affect index in the replication sample (with 95% CI) and report the original study's alpha of .93.
steps.quote: Responses of those items were averaged to gain a single affect index, which reached an internal consistency of α = .93. ... we analyzed the internal consistency of our affect index items and found α = .96 (95% CI [0.95, 0.97]).

steps.summary: Compute Cronbach's alpha for the 16-item German NFC scale in the replication sample with 95% CI.
steps.quote: In our sample and using the scale by Bless et al. (1994), we found a value of α = 0.85 (95% CI [0.83, 0.88], 16 items).

steps.summary: Run a one-way ANOVA of remembered expectation (BK03_07) on the induced expectation condition and report F, p and significance.
steps.quote: A one-way ANOVA revealed a significant influence of induced expectation on remembered expectations, F(2, 249) = 3.90, p = .021.

steps.summary: Run Tukey HSD post-hoc comparisons of remembered expectation means between the positive and negative expectation groups; report group means, SDs, Ns, the mean difference, its 95% CI and the p-value.
steps.quote: only a significant difference between the positive (M = 5.21, SD = 2.00, N = 75) and the negative (M = 4.35, SD = 1.94, N = 94) expectation group was found (Δ = 0.862, 95% CI [0.127, 1.597], p = .017).

steps.summary: Report the descriptive statistics (mean, SD, N) for the control/no-expectation group's remembered expectation.
steps.quote: The control group's values were between the other two groups (M = 4.63, SD = 2.11, N = 83).

steps.summary: Create a violin/jitter plot of remembered expectation by induced expectation condition (Figure 1), with solid lines representing medians.
steps.quote: A distribution of the data can be seen in Figure 1. Figure 1 Remembered expectation by induced expectation. Solid lines represent medians.

steps.summary: Fit a linear regression of affect index on expectation condition, NFC and their interaction; report the overall model F, p and R-squared and its significance.
steps.quote: The overall model test was not significant, F(5, 246) = 1.86, p = .103, R2 = 0.036.

steps.summary: Report that none of the model's individual effects were significant (all ps > .143).
steps.quote: In line with this, none of the model's effects were significant (all ps > .143, see Table 2).

steps.summary: Produce Table 2, the linear regression of affective reaction on expectation, NFC and their interaction, reporting the coefficient B, SE, t and p for all terms.
steps.quote: Table 2 Linear Regression of Affective Reaction on Expectation, NFC, and Their Interaction Coefficient B SE t p Intercept 1.88 1.44 1.31 .192 Expectation (none) 2.53 2.10 1.21 .229 Expectation (positive) 1.36 2.04 0.67 .506 NFC 0.42 0.29 1.47 .143 Expectation (none) × NFC −0.55 0.42 −1.32 .190 Expectation (positive) × NFC −0.13 0.41 −0.32 .750

steps.summary: Report the residual standard error (2.30 on 246 df) and the adjusted R-squared (.017) from the full regression model.
steps.quote: Residual SE = 2.30 on 246 df. R² = .036, adjusted R² = .017, F(5, 246) = 1.86, p = .103.

steps.summary: Run a two-way ANOVA of affect index on expectation condition and NFC (and their interaction); report F, p, eta-squared and the 90% CI for the expectation main effect, the NFC main effect and the interaction, and conclude there is no evidence for a group difference nor NFC moderation.
steps.quote: there was no main effect of expectation condition on the affect index, F(2, 246) = 3.00, p = .051, η² = 0.02, 90% CI [0, 0.05], need for cognition F(1, 246) = 1.43, p = .233, η² < 0.01, 90% CI [0, 0.02] or an interaction effect F(2, 246) = 0.92, p = .398, η² < 0.01, 90% CI [0, 0.02].

steps.summary: For each expectation condition (positive, negative, none), fit a simple linear regression of affect index on NFC and report the slope b, SE, t and p.
steps.quote: Positive expectations: b = 0.288, se = 0.306, t(73) = 0.94, p = .349 • Negative expectations: b = 0.420, se = 0.275, t(92) = 1.53, p = .130 • Control group (no specific expectations): b = -0.131, se = 0.312, t(81) = -0.420, p = .675.

steps.summary: Create a scatter plot with linear regression lines (with 95% confidence bands) of affect index on need for cognition for each expectation condition (Figure 2).
steps.quote: An overview of the results is presented in Figure 2 and Table 3. Figure 2 Regression lines predicting affect scores from need for cognition and expectation condition.

steps.summary: Produce Table 3 comparing original and replication results for the interaction test and the three expectation-condition slopes, with interpretations according to LeBel et al. (2019).
steps.quote: Table 3 Comparison of original and replication results with interpretations according to LeBel et al. (2019).

steps.summary: Create a histogram of the affect index scores (Figure 3).
steps.quote: Figure 3 Distribution of Affect Index Scores. N = 252.

steps.summary: Create a histogram of the need for cognition scores (Figure 4).
steps.quote: Figure 4 Distribution of Need for Cognition Scores. N = 252.

steps.summary: Convert the focal original (eta2=.04, N=160) and replication (eta2<.01, N=252) effect sizes to r=sqrt(eta2) and fit a fixed-effects meta-analytic moderator model (Lakens, 2022) with study as moderator; report the replication coefficient, QM and p.
steps.quote: effect sizes for the focal original and replication test were converted from η² to r and compared using a meta-analytical test for moderation by the replication. Thereby, the replication effect was significantly smaller than the original effect. ... The moderator test QM(1) = 4.09, p = .043 indicates the replication effect size differed significantly from the original.

steps.summary: Run a one-way ANOVA of affect index on expectation condition and report the F statistic and p-value.
steps.quote: Mean differences between the three expectation conditions did not differ overall, F(2, 249) = 3.00, p = .052.

steps.summary: Create a violin/jitter plot of affect index scores by expectation condition (Figure 5).
steps.quote: Figure 5 Affect scores by expectation condition. Solid lines represent medians.

steps.summary: Count participants by number of correctly identified movie statements (4, 3, 2, 1, missing), compute the percentages, and confirm no participant got all four statements wrong.
steps.quote: 149 participants (59.13%) identified all statements correctly, 77 (30.56%) identified 3/4, 22 (8.73%) identified 2/4, and 3 (1.19%) only identified 1/4 (1 missing value, 0.40%). No participant got all four statements wrong.

steps.summary: Re-run the main hypothesis model on the 149 participants who answered all four attention check items correctly; report F, p and R-squared.
steps.quote: Running the main hypothesis's model only on the 149 participants that responded correctly to the four attention check items did not affect the results, F(5, 143) = 0.94, p = .459, R² = .032.

steps.summary: Report the replication and original sample sizes (Nreplication=252, Noriginal=160) and the approximate statistical power (~80%) in the discussion.
steps.quote: a lack of statistical power (~80%) may have led to a non-significant finding (false-negative) though our sample size is considerably larger than the original (Nreplication= 252, Noriginal = 160).

steps.summary: Report the preregistered target sample size (400) and that the achieved sample still had >80% power for the original effect.
steps.quote: We did not achieve our preregistered target sample size for N = 400 participants but only N = 252, which still had >80% power for the original effect.

steps.summary: Report the recommended minimum sample size (N ≥ 400) for future studies.
steps.quote: use a very large sample size (N ≥ 400).

steps.summary: Collect all reproduced results and write outputs/results.json (format: schemas/results-output.schema.json); save figures to outputs/figures/<target id>.png
